title: The Vision
lede: The world fusion could help build: an advanced society powered cleanly while the living planet is given room to heal.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.
Why hold a vision at all

Engineering is disciplined by numbers, but it is aimed by a picture of the world it is trying to reach. Kronos keeps its technical work honest and its ambition explicit, and refuses to blur the line between the two. This page, and the pages linked from it, are the explicit picture. Everything here is labeled as vision so it is never mistaken for a specification.

The picture is simple to state. Human civilization keeps advancing — more computation, more medicine, more mobility, more people living well — while the atmosphere, the oceans, the forests, and the wild places recover rather than degrade. Historically those two goals have pulled against each other, because progress was paid for by burning things. Abundant clean energy is the hinge that lets both move in the same direction.

A vision is only worth stating if it names its conditions. For this one, clean energy has to become both abundant and firm — available at scale, and available on demand rather than only when the wind blows. It has to complement renewables instead of competing with them. And it has to arrive without a large new environmental burden of its own: no meltdown risk, little long-lived waste, minimal water, a small land footprint, and fuel that does not require mining.

The environment, health, and safety pages of this site make the honest, present-day case for each of those properties. This section extends that case forward in time and asks: if the properties hold, what world do they make available? Read the pages that follow as a set of if-then statements, not as guarantees.
Every page here is labeled as vision and separated from the technical safety case.
No economics appear anywhere — no prices, costs, or returns.
Frozen technical numbers, where cited, carry their real conditions.
The endgame is a balance, not a utopia: an advanced society and a recovering planet, held together by clean firm power.
Start with abundant clean energy, then follow the arc through a healed planet to the closing synthesis, a balanced world.

title: Abundant Clean Energy
lede: If fusion delivers firm power at scale, energy stops being the scarce input that everything else is rationed against.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

Almost every hard trade-off in modern life traces back to energy being scarce, dirty, or both. Fresh water is limited because desalination is energy-hungry. Recycling is limited because reprocessing materials costs energy. Clean industry is limited because high-temperature heat has meant combustion. When clean energy is abundant, each of these ceilings lifts at once.

Abundance here does not mean infinite or free. It means clean firm generation that can be added where and when it is needed, without a proportional rise in emissions, water use, or land disturbance. That combination — clean and firm and scalable — is what fusion is being designed to add to a grid that renewables are already decarbonizing.

A grid can be cheaply decarbonized to a point on wind, solar, and storage alone. Past that point, the last increment of reliability — the calm, dark winter week — becomes the expensive, dirty part, and is often met by keeping fossil plants on standby. Firm clean power fills exactly that role: steady output that holds the grid up when variable sources are quiet, so the fossil backstop can finally be retired.

Kronos is designed to be that firm partner rather than a replacement for renewables. The two machines occupy different niches — the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) for direct, on-site electricity, the breeder (Hyperion) as the tritium and neutron foundation — but both point toward the same outcome: capability without a combustion bill.
This is contingent: it assumes the machines reach the performance their designs target.
Today they are simulation studies; first breeder construction is planned for Q2 2027.
Abundance is a direction of travel, not a delivered fact.

title: Powering Advanced Intelligence, Cleanly
lede: Large-scale computation is becoming a defining human capability — and its growing appetite for power can be met without a growing emissions bill.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. Compute is the new heavy industry

Training and running large models, simulating proteins and plasmas, rendering weather and climate at fine resolution — all of it runs on electricity, and the demand is rising steeply. Left on a fossil grid, that demand becomes a large new source of emissions. On clean firm power, the same growth in capability arrives without the carbon.

Data centers are unusual loads: they run flat-out around the clock and cannot tolerate interruption. That profile is a poor match for variable generation alone and a natural match for firm clean power delivered on site. The burner housing MetroVolt is aimed squarely at this case — direct energy conversion to electricity, sited where the compute is.

There is a further link worth naming. The same computation that fusion powers is also what makes fusion tractable: surrogate models, plasma-control learning, and materials search all lean on large-scale compute. Advanced intelligence and clean energy can reinforce each other — better models design better machines, which power more capable models.
Kronos treats this as a working relationship, not a slogan. The AI and control stack that runs the plasma is the same class of system that the plant is designed to power for others.
Direct energy conversion in the burner is a design choice, not yet a demonstrated plant.
The burner is D–³He with a modest neutron fraction of 5.44%, still a simulation study today.

title: The Healed Planet
lede: The endgame is not merely lower emissions but a biosphere given the energy and the room to recover.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.
From doing less harm to doing repair

Most climate action so far has been about subtraction: emit less, use less, disturb less. Necessary, but subtraction alone leaves a damaged system to heal on its own. Abundant clean energy opens a second mode — active repair — because restoration is itself energy-intensive. Pulling carbon back out of the air, desalinating water to green arid land, and running clean industry all cost energy that has to come from somewhere clean.

A healed planet, in this vision, is one where the flows finally point the right way: forests expanding rather than shrinking, aquifers refilling, air clearing over cities, and the ocean chemistry stabilizing. None of that is fusion’s achievement alone. It is what becomes affordable in energy terms when firm clean power is abundant.

title: The Firm-Clean Pair
lede: Fusion and renewables are complements, not rivals: variable sources do the bulk decarbonization, firm clean power closes the reliability gap.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

A decarbonized grid has two distinct jobs. The first is producing enormous quantities of clean energy cheaply — the job wind and solar already do superbly and will keep doing. The second is being there at every hour regardless of weather — the job that variable sources, even with storage, do only up to a point. Treating these as one contest has produced a false choice.

Firm clean generation is built for the second job. It does not out-compete a solar farm at noon; it holds the grid up during the windless, sunless stretch that would otherwise be covered by gas. In that division of labor, more firm clean power means more renewables can be deployed, because their weak hours finally have a clean answer.

Why not just build more batteries

Storage is essential and expands every year, but it shifts energy across hours, not comfortably across a still, overcast week. Covering rare long lulls with storage alone means building vast capacity that sits idle most of the time. Firm generation covers those lulls with a steady source instead, which is why serious decarbonization plans keep a firm clean component in the mix.
Kronos is designed to be that component. The intent is partnership with the renewable buildout, not competition with it.

title: Firm Power for a Renewable Grid
lede: The hardest part of a clean grid is the last increment of reliability; firm fusion is designed to supply exactly that.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

Getting a grid to a high share of clean energy is increasingly routine. Getting it to a fully clean, always-on grid runs into a stubborn tail: the small fraction of hours each year when demand is high and wind and solar are both low. That tail is disproportionately expensive to cover with variable sources and storage, and it is where fossil plants tend to survive.

Firm clean generation is the natural tool for the tail. Because it runs on demand rather than on weather, a relatively modest firm fleet can retire a much larger standby fossil fleet. The vision is a grid whose last dirty megawatt-hours are finally displaced.

Firm generation is also compact. A plant that produces steady output from a small footprint can sit near load — a city, a port, a cluster of data centers — reducing the need for long new transmission lines across contested landscapes. The burner (Aegis / MetroVolt) is conceived for exactly this kind of sited, on-demand role.
Compactness is an environmental property in its own right: less land disturbed, fewer corridors cut, more of the map left to nature. See rewilding and land for that thread.
The tail-filling role is a design intent, not a proven capability today.
First breeder construction is planned for Q2 2027; burner testing is later.

title: Energy and the Good Life
lede: Abundant clean power is not an end in itself; it is what lets people live well and live closer to nature at the same time.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

It is easy to talk about megawatts and forget what they are for. Energy is comfortable homes, preserved food, clean water from a tap, a hospital that never loses power, a child studying after dark, mobility that does not choke a city in smog. The good life, for most of human history, has been rationed by how much clean energy a society could muster.

The vision is not more consumption for its own sake. It is decoupling well-being from harm: the same warmth, light, water, and mobility, delivered without the emissions and pollution that have always come attached. When the energy is clean and firm, raising the floor of everyday life stops meaning raising the ecological toll.

Closer to nature, not further from it

A common assumption is that a high-energy society must be a paved-over one. The opposite is possible. Compact firm generation, electrified transport, and clean industry free up land and clear the air, making it easier to live among green space rather than apart from it. Cities that breathe, rivers left in their channels, quiet streets — these are energy outcomes as much as design ones.
This is the human center of the vision: technology in service of an unhurried, healthier daily life, on a planet that is recovering rather than declining.
This is an aspiration about outcomes, not a claim any plant delivers it today.
The machines are simulation studies; the timeline is generational.
No economic claims are made or implied here.

title: Water Abundance
lede: Fresh water is scarce mainly because making it costs energy; abundant clean power turns desalination and reuse from last resorts into everyday tools.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

Two-thirds of the planet is water, yet fresh water is one of the most contested resources on Earth. The reason is energy: desalinating seawater, recycling wastewater, and moving water uphill to where people live all take power. Where power is scarce or dirty, clean water is rationed, rivers are over-drawn, and aquifers are mined faster than they refill.

With abundant clean firm energy, that constraint loosens. Coastal desalination and inland water reuse become routine rather than emergency measures, so cities can be supplied without draining the rivers and wetlands that ecosystems depend on. The vision is water security that does not come at nature’s expense.

A note on the plant itself

There is a second water angle worth stating plainly. Because the burner uses direct energy conversion rather than a steam cycle, it is designed to need very little cooling water — unlike thermal plants that evaporate large volumes. The safety-case section covers this in detail; the vision simply notes that clean-water abundance should not be undercut by thirsty generation.
The abundance case is contingent on clean energy at scale, still to be proven.
Desalination has its own siting and brine-management considerations, handled elsewhere.

lede: Most urban air pollution is combustion; replacing the burning with clean electricity clears the air people breathe every day.

The air is made of choices

Smog, soot, and the fine particulate that shortens millions of lives each year are not natural facts. They are the exhaust of burning things — fuel in engines, gas in boilers, coal and gas in power plants. Every one of those combustion sources has a clean electric alternative, and the barrier to switching has been the supply of clean, firm, affordable electricity.

In the vision, cities run on that supply. Vehicles are electric, buildings are heated with clean electricity, and the power itself carries no smokestack. The immediate reward is not abstract: it is air that is safe to breathe, skies that are clear, and a measurable fall in respiratory and cardiovascular disease.

title: Restoring the Carbon Balance
lede: Cutting emissions to zero stops the problem growing; abundant clean energy is what makes pulling legacy carbon back out affordable in energy terms.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. Stabilizing the climate involves two separate tasks. The first is stopping new emissions — the decarbonization already underway. The second is drawing down the carbon already in the atmosphere from a century of burning. The second task is often left out because it is energy-intensive: capturing dilute carbon dioxide from the air and fixing it takes real power.

On a fossil grid, running carbon removal is self-defeating. On an abundant clean grid, it becomes a legitimate tool — clean energy spent to reverse damage rather than to cause it. The vision includes this drawdown phase, not as fusion’s achievement alone but as something abundant firm power makes feasible.

Carbon drawdown at planetary scale is an enormous undertaking and Kronos claims no special role in the capture technology itself. The honest statement is narrow: removal is bounded by clean energy supply, and firm clean generation raises that bound. Whether and how fast humanity uses the headroom is a societal choice, not a technical guarantee.

title: Energy for Everyone
lede: A billion people still lack reliable electricity; compact firm clean generation could extend modern energy without repeating the fossil path.

Reliable electricity is the quiet prerequisite for health, education, and opportunity, and hundreds of millions of people still live without it or with an unreliable supply. Historically, closing that gap meant building fossil infrastructure — the same path the industrialized world took, with the same emissions and pollution attached.

The vision is a different path for the still-electrifying world: clean firm power that does not lock in decades of emissions. Compact generation that can be sited near where people live, paired with the falling cost of renewables, could bring modern energy without repeating the mistakes that got the atmosphere into trouble.

title: The Long Horizon

One reason visions lose credibility is that they collapse near and far into a single breathless promise. Kronos keeps them separate. title: Fusion and the Reach into Space
lede: The same fuels and physics that power a clean planet also point outward — helium-3, deep-space power, and a lunar link that closes back onto Earth.

The burner runs on deuterium and helium-3. Helium-3 is rare on Earth but comparatively abundant in the lunar regolith, which is why fusion and space exploration have long been linked in serious long-range thinking. In the vision, that link runs both ways: space capability helps supply fusion fuel, and fusion helps power the reach into space.

The breeder (Hyperion) is relevant here too. Among its designed products is helium-3 at roughly 1.97 kg/yr class output, alongside its tritium-class production. A terrestrial helium-3 source and a lunar one are complementary parts of the same long-horizon fuel picture.

Every energy source has a footprint

Land is a finite resource that agriculture, cities, and energy all compete for. Fossil extraction scars it; even clean sources use space — solar farms and wind arrays trade a large area for their clean output. title: The Electrified World
lede: The cleanest path for most of the economy is to electrify it and make the electricity clean; abundant firm power is what makes that switch complete.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

The decarbonization strategy that keeps proving out is simple to name: move transport, heating, and as much industry as possible from burning fuel to running on electricity, and make that electricity clean. Electric systems are efficient and controllable, and once the grid is clean, everything plugged into it becomes clean at a stroke.

The limit on this strategy has always been the supply of clean, firm electricity to plug into. As loads that used to burn fuel move onto the grid, demand rises sharply, and only a clean firm supply can meet it without reopening the emissions gap. That is the role fusion is designed to add.

title: Industry Without Smoke
lede: Heavy industry runs on high-temperature heat that has meant combustion; clean electricity and clean fuels can supply that heat without the smokestack.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

Steel, cement, chemicals, and glass are the backbone of the built world and among the hardest sectors to decarbonize, because they need intense, sustained heat that has traditionally come from burning coal and gas. This is the industrial core that many climate plans treat as a stubborn remainder.

Abundant clean firm power changes what is feasible. Electric furnaces, clean hydrogen for chemical reduction, and process heat from clean electricity can each displace combustion in parts of this core. None is trivial, and each is energy-hungry — which is exactly why they wait on a clean firm supply large enough to feed them.

title: From Scarcity to Abundance
lede: The mindset shift the vision asks for: treating energy as something that can be abundant and clean, rather than a fixed budget to be fought over.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

Much of energy policy is framed as budgeting: a fixed, scarce quantity to be divided among competing uses, with every gain for one sector a loss for another. That framing is realistic while clean energy is genuinely scarce. It becomes a self-imposed limit if clean firm energy can be made abundant.

The vision asks for a shift from budget to flow — from rationing a scarce clean resource to expanding it. This does not mean waste; abundance and efficiency go together, because efficient systems make abundance go further. It means stopping the assumption that living well and living cleanly must trade against each other.

Framing is not idle. A scarcity mindset produces zero-sum politics around energy: growth versus climate, one region versus another, this decade versus the next. An abundance mindset, if it is warranted by the technology, dissolves several of those conflicts at once. The responsibility is to make sure the mindset is earned by real clean supply, not asserted ahead of it.

title: Energy Without Emissions
lede: The core promise of fusion is decoupling energy from the smokestack: capability that does not add carbon or combustion pollution to the air.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

Since the industrial revolution, more energy has meant more combustion, and more combustion has meant more carbon dioxide and pollution. That link is so old it can feel like a law of nature. It is not. It is an artifact of how we have made energy, and it can be broken by making energy differently.

Fusion breaks the link at the source. The reaction releases energy from light nuclei rather than from burning carbon, so there is no carbon dioxide and no combustion exhaust from the generation itself. The burner’s direct energy conversion turns that reaction into electricity without a fire and without a steam plume.

No energy source is free of all impact: building any plant uses materials and energy, and fusion has its own considerations, covered candidly in the safety and waste sections — low activation, a favorable waste class, no long-lived spent fuel. title: Oceans and Fusion
lede: The ocean absorbs our carbon and our heat; ending combustion and easing the pressure on rivers gives marine systems room to stabilize.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.
The sea has been the buffer

The ocean has quietly absorbed a large share of the carbon dioxide and heat from two centuries of burning, which is why it is warming and acidifying. That buffering has spared the atmosphere worse, at the cost of the marine chemistry that reefs, shellfish, and fisheries depend on. Relieving the ocean means turning off the carbon at the source.

Clean energy that emits no carbon does exactly that. As generation and industry stop adding carbon dioxide, the pressure that drives ocean acidification eases, giving marine ecosystems a chance to stabilize rather than degrade further. This is slow — ocean chemistry has long memory — but the direction reverses.

There is a second ocean link. Clean desalination can supply coastal cities from the sea instead of from over-drawn rivers and aquifers, protecting the freshwater ecosystems that suffer when human demand outstrips supply. And because the burner needs little cooling water, firm clean generation does not add its own thirst to the problem.

title: Energy and Isotopes for Medicine
lede: Beyond electricity, fusion machines produce neutrons and isotopes that medicine relies on — a health dividend alongside the clean-power one.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

A fusion machine is a source of energetic neutrons and, by design, of specific isotopes. The breeder (Hyperion) is a deuterium–tritium spherical tokamak whose designed products include 14 MeV neutrons and a tritium-class output, alongside helium-3. Those outputs have uses far beyond the grid, and medicine is among the most important.

Medical imaging and certain cancer treatments depend on a reliable supply of specific isotopes, several of which are today produced in ageing reactors and are prone to shortage. A neutron source designed for steady operation could help stabilize that supply — a public-health benefit that rides alongside the energy mission.

title: The Post-Combustion Era
lede: The through-line of the vision is the end of burning things for energy — a civilizational shift as large as the one that started with fire.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.
Fire built us; fire also limits us

Controlled fire is arguably humanity’s oldest technology, and burning fuel has powered every advance since the industrial revolution. But combustion is also the root of the climate problem, of urban air pollution, and of much geopolitical conflict over fuel. The post-combustion era is the idea that we can keep the capability fire gave us while retiring the fire itself.

Fusion is not fire. It releases energy by combining light nuclei, not by oxidizing carbon, so it produces no carbon dioxide and no smoke. Together with renewables and electrification, it points toward an energy system where nothing needs to be burned to keep the lights on, the factories running, or the vehicles moving.

What ends, and what does not
Ends: routine burning of coal, oil, and gas for power, heat, and transport.
Ends: the air pollution and carbon that combustion carries.
Continues: the capability — warmth, mobility, industry, computation — now clean.
Continues: renewables as the bulk supply, with firm fusion closing the gap.

This is a long-horizon, civilization-scale claim, and it is offered as a direction rather than a schedule. The machines are simulation studies; the transition is the work of decades and of many technologies together. Naming the destination is how the near-term engineering stays pointed the right way.

title: Resilience and Energy Security
lede: Energy made from abundant, widely available fuel and produced near where it is used is harder to disrupt and less bound to geopolitics.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. A great deal of geopolitical friction comes from where fossil fuels happen to lie in the ground. Nations that lack them import them; nations that have them wield them. Energy security, for most of the world, has meant securing access to fuel from somewhere else, with all the vulnerability that implies.

Fusion’s primary fuel is deuterium, extracted from ordinary water and available to essentially every nation with a coastline or a water supply. The breeder is designed to make its own tritium, and helium-3 can be bred rather than mined. A fuel base this distributed changes the security picture: there is no single chokepoint to control.

title: Computing and Discovery
lede: Clean power and large-scale computation form a loop: energy runs the models, and the models accelerate the science, including fusion itself.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

Whole fields now advance at the pace of available computation. Protein structures, new materials, climate projections, and drug candidates are increasingly found by simulation and machine learning before they are ever made in a lab. The rate of discovery is, in part, an energy question: more clean compute means more searching of the space of possible answers.

Fusion sits inside this loop in an unusual way. The same class of computation that fusion could power is also what makes fusion itself tractable: surrogate models that run design studies orders of magnitude faster than first-principles solvers, and control systems that learn to hold a plasma steady. Kronos builds and uses this stack directly.

title: The Fuel That Doesn’t Run Out
lede: Fusion’s fuels are drawn from water and bred in the machine, not dug from a mine — a supply that does not deplete on any human timescale.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

The breeder runs on deuterium and tritium. Deuterium is a heavy form of hydrogen present in ordinary water — every liter of seawater contains it, and the total in the oceans is effectively inexhaustible on any human timescale. Tritium is not mined at all: the breeder is designed to make its own, treating the tritium breeding ratio as a design lever across 1.1, 1.5, and 1.8.

The burner runs on deuterium and helium-3. Helium-3 is rare terrestrially, but it too can be bred rather than mined — the breeder is designed to produce it in a helium-3 output class alongside its tritium. In both machines, the fuel story avoids the extraction, transport, and geopolitics that fossil fuels carry.

title: Cities That Breathe
lede: Freed from combustion and its footprint, cities can weave nature back through the built environment rather than paving it out.

Cities have long been treated as the opposite of nature — the place where the wild is pushed out. That framing was partly forced by combustion: power plants, traffic, and industry made dense living dirty and loud, and green space was a scarce amenity rather than a structural feature. Clean, quiet, firm energy loosens that constraint.

When power is clean and generation is compact and near load, more of the urban fabric can be given to parks, street trees, green roofs, and daylit rivers. A city that no longer burns is a city that can breathe — cooler in summer, cleaner to inhale, and richer in the small pockets of habitat that make dense living pleasant.

It is a claim that density and nature are compatible once the dirty, land-hungry parts of the energy system shrink. The land a compact grid does not need, and the air a clean grid does not foul, are exactly the resources a livable city has always lacked.
Urban form is a planning choice; clean energy enables it but does not decide it.

title: The Generational Project

Some projects are finished by the people who start them. This one is not. Bringing fusion from design studies to a fleet of plants, and then to the abundance this section describes, spans more time than any single working life. Pretending otherwise would be a form of dishonesty — the kind that erodes trust when the fast timeline fails to arrive.

So Kronos states it plainly: this is a generational project. The near-term milestones are real and dated — construction planned for Q2 2027, first tritium targeted around 2030 — but the endgame is a relay handed across generations of engineers, scientists, and builders. Each generation’s job is to move the work honestly to the next.

title: Energy and Biodiversity
lede: Habitat loss and climate change are the two great pressures on wild life; clean, compact, firm energy eases both at once.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

The decline of wild species is driven above all by two forces: the conversion of habitat to human use, and the shifting of climate faster than ecosystems can adapt. Energy sits behind both — land taken for extraction and generation, and warming driven by combustion. A clean, compact, firm energy system reduces both pressures with the same move.

Compact generation frees land that can stay or become habitat. Zero-carbon generation slows the warming that pushes species out of their ranges. Neither is sufficient alone; together they change the trajectory that wildlife faces. The vision counts biodiversity as a first-class outcome of getting energy right, not an afterthought.

Beyond easing pressure, active restoration — replanting, rewetting drained land, running conservation infrastructure — takes energy and clean water. Abundant clean power makes those efforts affordable in energy terms, turning conservation from a defensive holding action into something that can expand habitat rather than merely defend it.
Biodiversity depends on many factors beyond energy; this is one lever among several.
Freed land is rewilded only if societies choose to; the technology creates the option.

title: Restoring Nature
lede: The active repair of ecosystems — forests, wetlands, soils — becomes possible at scale when the energy to do the work is clean and abundant.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.
Repair is work, and work needs energy

Letting nature recover on its own is slow and, in degraded landscapes, sometimes impossible. Active restoration — replanting forests, rewetting drained peatlands, rebuilding soils, removing invasive species, restoring rivers — is real physical work that takes machinery, water, and logistics, all of which take energy. On a scarce or dirty energy budget, restoration competes with everything else and usually loses.

With abundant clean energy, restoration stops being a luxury. The same firm clean power that runs cities can run the pumps, vehicles, nurseries, and desalination that large-scale ecological repair depends on. The vision treats a recovering biosphere not as passive hope but as an active project that clean energy underwrites.

Restoration is ecological work with its own science and its own failures; energy removes one constraint, not all of them. And the choice to restore is a human one. Kronos’s claim is bounded: abundant clean energy makes large-scale repair affordable in energy terms, turning a hard constraint into a solvable one. title: The Endgame: A Balanced World
lede: The destination is not a utopia but a balance — an advanced society and a recovering planet, held together by clean firm power.
body: Vision, not specification. This page describes a future that fusion could help make possible — not a product promise, forecast, or performance claim. The Kronos machines today are design and simulation studies: the breeder (Hyperion) and the burner (Aegis / MetroVolt). No hardware net-gain has been demonstrated; construction of the first breeder is planned to begin in Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium targeted around 2030.

It would be easy, and wrong, to end this section with a promise of paradise. The honest endgame is more modest and more durable: a balance. A civilization that keeps advancing — in computation, medicine, mobility, and comfort — while the living systems it depends on recover rather than decline. Two curves that used to trade against each other, finally moving the same way.

Everything in this section converges here. Abundant clean energy lifts the ceilings that scarcity imposed; firm clean power retires combustion; compact generation returns land to nature; clean water and carbon drawdown make active repair affordable. None of it is fusion alone, and none of it is guaranteed. All of it is what becomes possible if clean firm energy stops being scarce.

The picture is why the narrow work matters. Each milestone is a step toward a world that does not force a choice between human flourishing and a living planet.
